results.title: Benjamini–Hochberg Procedure | Statsig Docs
results.content: Benjamini–Hochberg Procedure | Statsig Docs The Benjamini-Hochberg Procedure ("BH" procedure) is a statistical method that reduces the probability of false positives by adjusting the significance level for multiple comparisons. It is not as extreme as a Bonferroni Correction, because instead of controlling the chance of at least one false positive (Family Wise Error Rate), BH controls the expected value of false positives when the null hypothesis has been rejected (False Discovery Rate). Like with many other analysis settings, you can enable BH procedure for individual experiments (or configure global Experiment Settings to default it). : Benjamini-Hochberg procedure configuration interface The Benjamini-Hochberg Procedure updates the significance level to be used (modifying your pre-set α\alpha α). The new significance level to be applied is calculated by sorting the p-values of metrics in ascending order and comparing with a paired threshold. Each p-value’s paired threshold is the desired False Discovery Rate divided by the number of comparisons being evaluated multiplied by what rank a p-value is in the ordered list. The largest threshold value which is higher than its corresponding p-value is our new significance level (α\alpha α). The Benjamini-Hochberg Procedure can be applied based on: * The number of test groups (multiple treatment hypotheses). For each metric aggregate the list of p-values from each variant and complete the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. * The number of metrics in the scorecard. For each variant aggregate the list of p-values from each metric and complete the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. * Both the number of test groups and number of metrics in the scorecard. All p-values are aggregated to complete the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. Statsig does not apply BH procedure when evaluating the p-values of any event-dimension or user-property experiment metric results. Only the top-line metric results are compared to the new significance level. Last updated on **Sep 18, 2025**

results.title: Benjamini-Hochberg Correction - MetricGate Calculator
results.content: Try our Benjamini-Hochberg Calculator to control the false discovery rate in your multiple hypothesis tests. # Benjamini-Hochberg Procedure (False Discovery Rate Control). The Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure is a powerful method for controlling the False Discovery Rate (FDR) in multiple hypothesis testing. Unlike the Bonferroni or Holm corrections, which control the probability of any false positives (family-wise error rate), the BH procedure focuses on controlling the expected proportion of false positives among all rejected hypotheses. Suppose you run *m* hypothesis tests and obtain p-values *p(1), ..., p(m)* sorted in ascending order. 2. For each p-value *p(i)*, calculate the threshold: \dfrac{i}{m} \cdot \alpha. The BH procedure is especially suited to exploratory research and large-scale testing scenarios where FDR control is more appropriate than family-wise error rate control. Suppose you have six p-values:. With \alpha = 0.05 and *m = 6* tests, the BH threshold for each rank *i* is \dfrac{i}{6} \cdot 0.05. # Benjamini-Hochberg FDR Correction Example in R # Simulated p-values from 6 hypothesis tests raw_pvalues <- c(0.005, 0.01, 0.04, 0.08, 0.12, 0.20) # Apply BH correction bh_adjusted <- p.adjust(raw_pvalues, method = "BH") # Compile results results <- data.frame( Test = paste0("H", 1:6), Raw_P = raw_pvalues, BH_Adjusted_P = round(bh_adjusted, 3), Significant = bh_adjusted < 0.05 ) # Print results print(results) # Optional visualization barplot( bh_adjusted, names.arg = results$Test, col = ifelse(results$Significant, "red", "gray"), ylab = "Adjusted P-value", main = "Benjamini-Hochberg Adjusted P-values" ) abline(h = 0.05, col = "blue", lty = 2) legend("topright", legend = c("Significant", "Not Significant"), fill = c("red", "gray")). After applying the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, two hypotheses (H1 and H2) are flagged as statistically significant at the 5% FDR threshold. * **Significant:** H1 and H2 have BH-adjusted p-values of 0.03 → we reject the null hypothesis for these comparisons, controlling the expected proportion of false discoveries. * **Not Significant:** H3 to H6 have adjusted p-values between 0.08 and 0.20 → we do not reject their null hypotheses. This demonstrates the strength of BH correction: it allows more discoveries (H1 and H2) than stricter methods like Bonferroni, while still controlling the false discovery rate across all comparisons. * **Does not guarantee zero false positives:** It controls the proportion, not the presence, of false discoveries.

results.content: Recall that the Holm-Bonferroni method, which we discussed in the first blog post, controls the FWER at a specified level \(\alpha\) (a common choice is \(\alpha = 0.05\)) for *any* set of null hypotheses, even if those hypotheses are not independent of each other.3, then the hypotheses \(H_i\) will only be independent of each other if the random variables \(X_i\) are independent of each other."). Each time we do the experiment we test the same \(m\) hypotheses, and we evaluate the significance of our results using either a FDR-controlling method or a FWER-controlling method. If we do these 100 experiments and interpret them using a method that controls the FWER, then we will find that we rejected at least one true null hypothesis in about \(100\cdot\alpha\) experiments (so about 5 cases if \(\alpha = 0.05\)).4  instead of exactly that number is that we have a finite sample of experiments, so the observed proportion of these experiments where \(V \geq 1\) will approach, but not be exactly equal to, the true probability \(P(V\geq 1)\).

results.content: Unlike very strict methods such as the Bonferroni correction, which try to eliminate all false positives, the BH method aims to control the False Discovery Rate (FDR), which is the expected proportion of false positives among the results that are considered significant. * ****Step 1:**** Collect all p-values from your tests. Step-by-Step Explanation of the BH Procedure Suppose we perform m hypothesis tests and obtain m p-values. results.title: Benjamini–Hochberg correction, FDR in genes' expressions
results.content: Benjamini–Hochberg correction, FDR in genes' expressions. The un-corrected P-values are in the range of 0.015 - 0.05 (significant per alpha 0.05). Now when I apply Benjamini–Hochberg correction, there are few (<10) differentially expressed genes left with corrected-P <0.05 (or FDR<0.05). Theoretically, the FDR is applied to control/minimize the falsely discovered un-corrected Ps (which may be by chance, given the alpha 0.05). I am not a statistician and I don't feel prepared to explain in detail why, but I can refer you to this interesting page for a general overview on the topic. 2.7 years ago by. 2.7 years ago by. As mentioned above, the large reduction in differentially expressed genes (DEGs) is not unexpected. Less stringent corrections for the sake of increasing the number of overall number of DEGs will just reduce confidence in the result, but something like independent hypothesis weighting, which prioritizes highly expressed genes may help (In R, you can use the package `iwh`, see vignette). 2.7 years ago by. Under a nominal p-value threshold of 0.05, if we test 20,000 genes, we would expect 1000 false positives on average (this is only on average, and we can say how many there will be in a given study). Thus, if you found 1,100 genes differentially expressed, we would expect 91% (1000/1100) of the hits to be false positives. Under a BH correction we reduce the p-value threshold until we expect only 5% of the positives to be false positives. If you only found 100 DE genes at a nominal p-value threshold of 0.05, this is fewer than the number of false positives we expect to find even if there are no true positives. In fact, the fact that you have so many fewer genes significant at the nominal threshold than you might expect would make me wonder if there was something wrong with the analysis. It should either be relatively uniform, with equal numbers of genes in each pvalue bin (suggesting there is no difference between your samples), or it should make an enrichment of genes at low pvalues (suggesting a real signal that you are not sufficiently powered to assign to particular genes). 2.7 years ago by.
